summary: Describes general definitions and mechanisms for establishing Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespaces. A URN namespace gives a family of identifiers their own rules. It is a best current practice that replaces RFC 2611 and was later replaced by RFC 8141.

eli5.summary: A permanent name is only useful if there are clear rules for how names in each family are made. This document says how to set up a new family of such names.

questions: how to register a urn namespace
what is the difference between formal and informal urn namespaces
subtitle: How a community gets its own family of permanent names, and a registered Namespace ID, from IANA.

tldr.problem: A URN is supposed to be a persistent name, but not every string that fits the URN syntax is a valid name, and not every syntactically valid namespace is a recognized one. Someone has to define how new namespaces come into being.
tldr.mechanism: A community fills in a registration template and obtains a Namespace ID (NID) from IANA. Three kinds of namespace exist (Experimental, Informal and Formal), each with its own registration route.
tldr.outcome: This best current practice replaced RFC 2611 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 8141, so it is no longer the current procedure.

today: RFC 3406 is a Best Current Practice that obsoleted RFC 2611 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8141, which is the document to read for the current URN namespace procedures.

sections.title: Why URN Namespaces Need Managing
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Names (URNs) are resource identifiers meant to identify a resource independent of its location and to last a long time. They belong to the URI family and aim at persistent naming of resources.

The RFC rests on two assumptions. First, assigning a URN is a managed process: not every string that fits the URN syntax is a valid URN, because each name is assigned under the rules of a particular namespace. Second, the space of namespaces is managed too: a namespace needs a recognized definition to be valid.

The document describes a mechanism and a template for defining a namespace, plus how to get an identifier for it (the Namespace ID, or NID) registered with IANA. It covers creating namespaces only. If names should also be resolvable, a separate registration in a global NID directory such as the DDDS system is needed.
sections.eli5: Not every made-up label counts as an official permanent name. There has to be a rulebook and an official list of the families of names.

sections.title: What a URN Namespace Is
sections.content:
For URNs, a namespace is a collection of uniquely assigned identifiers. An identifier is never assigned to more than one resource and never re-assigned to a different one. A single resource may still have more than one URN, for different purposes.

The namespace has its own identifier so that URNs are globally unique and, where desired, so that the identifier hints at its structure. The RFC points out that many systems use strings of numbers (ISBN, ISSN, phone numbers), and the same number could be valid in two of them. Separate namespace identifiers keep the resulting URNs different.

How a community designs its identifiers, assigns them and uses them is specific to that community and is outside the scope of the IETF URN work.
sections.eli5: Two schools might both have a student number 1234. Putting the school name in front keeps the two students from being mixed up.

sections.title: Experimental, Informal and Formal Namespaces
sections.content:
The RFC defines three categories, distinguished by the expected level of service and the registration procedure.

  • Experimental namespaces are not registered with IANA and take the form X-<NID>. Nothing prevents collisions, so they are for internal or limited experimental use.
  • Informal namespaces are fully fledged URN namespaces that can be registered in global registration services. They must provide persistent identification and unique assignment. IANA assigns the NID.
  • Formal namespaces involve IETF review and suit cases where publishing the namespace benefits some subset of Internet users. The namespace must be usable on the global Internet, though it may use a fee-based, privately managed or proprietary registry if the access protocols are openly published.

For a Formal request, the proposer must document the need for a new namespace and the community benefit, and give some thought to longevity. The URN working group listed things to look for: an organization that shows stability, competence in assigning names, and a commitment not to re-assign names or resolve them to false or stale information. The IESG may decline to publish a proposal if the IETF consensus is that it has technical flaws that would impair persistent identification.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of name families: a scratch pad for experiments, a family that gets a numbered label quickly, and an official family that must be reviewed because it will be used by lots of people.

sections.title: Registration Procedures
sections.content:
IANA keeps the official list of registered URN namespaces. The procedure depends on the type.

For an Informal namespace, IANA assigns the identifier urn-<number> on a First Come First Served basis; the number must consist strictly of digits and must not make the NID too long under the URN syntax. The registrant sends the completed template to the urn-nid discussion list, allows a 2 week discussion period, and then submits it to IANA. The original registrant, or someone they designate, can update the registration using the same steps.

For a Formal namespace, the NID is assigned by IETF Consensus, which means publishing an RFC through the normal process. The RFC need not be on the standards track, and the template can sit inside another RFC or stand alone. It must include a Namespace Considerations section (why existing namespaces fall short), a Community Considerations section (who benefits and how a general Internet user can take part) and an IANA Considerations section. The requested NID must not be already registered, must not start with x- or urn-, must not start with two ASCII letters followed by a hyphen, and must be more than 2 letters long. All two-letter combinations are reserved for possible country-code-based namespaces.
sections.eli5: For a quick family you mail in a form, wait two weeks for comments, and get a numbered label. For an official family you have to write it up as an RFC and convince the reviewers.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
Appendix A is a template that every namespace definition fills in. It asks for the Namespace ID, registration version and date (in YYYY-MM-DD form), the declared registrant, the syntactic structure of identifiers, relevant documentation, and several considerations: uniqueness, persistence, how identifiers are assigned, and how they are resolved.

It also asks for rules for lexical equivalence, conformance with URN syntax, a validation mechanism and the scope of the namespace. The template is meant to help people who want to be assigned URNs or run resolvers, and communities deciding whether to reuse part of an existing namespace.

Appendix B shows a filled-in example based on a hypothetical generic Internet namespace built from a fully-qualified domain name. The RFC itself notes that domain names can be re-assigned, which makes the example a poor URN namespace in practice, so it is not seriously proposed.
sections.eli5: The template is a questionnaire about your new name family: who runs it, how names look, and how you promise never to give the same name to two things.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it mostly deals with declaring public information, which should be of relatively low security profile. There is still a danger of spoofing and misinformation, so the information in these declarations should be taken as advisory.

For IANA, the appropriate NID is assigned once an IESG-designated expert has confirmed that the required registration steps are complete. The document defines processes that replace those in RFC 2611.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a form saying anything, so treat what is written as a helpful note, not a guarantee.
